catalog_locator: Sharma 2001, sect. 2.3 'Tonal Contrasts', p.280; supporting sentence sect. 2.1.1, p.272. Willis 2009 review, p.2 and p.3.
catalog_quote: 2.3 Tonal Contrasts. We have found a two-way tonal contrast in Byangsi, i.e. a high falling tone, transcribed with a grave accent mark on the vowel (/à/), and a level tone, which is left unmarked. The tones typically occur on the first syllable of multisyllabic words only. None of the earlier descriptions mentioned above recorded any tonal contrasts. The examples showing contrasts are given below: /ye/ 'an eagle type of bird' /yè/ 'mountain'; /khu/ 'family' /khù/ 'smoke'; /pi/ 'four' /pì-/ 'to sweep'; /ki-/ 'to twine' /kì-/ 'to break hard objects' ... Tone contrasts with long vowels: /ga:/ 'paddy' /gà:/ 'wound' [p.272] Phonetically the vowels with high falling tones are shorter than the vowels with level tones.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Byangsi is described as having a two-way lexical tone contrast (high-falling vs level) whose locus is the word-initial syllable of polysyllabic words; the sketch gives no statement at all about word stress/accent. The only fuller grammar by the same author (2007) likewise omits stress, as its reviewer (Willis 2009: 2) explicitly notes ('Sharma does not mention the stress pattern found in Byangsi'), implying a stress pattern exists but is undescribed in accessible sources.
new_statements.exceptions: 'typically.. on the first syllable.. only' (hedged); verb roots mostly high-falling; high-falling tone arises as compensation for loss of root-final vowel length in verb morphology (sect. 7). No stress exceptions because no stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms, elicited minimal pairs from three speakers of Nabi, Gunji and Napalchu villages, Dharchula tehsil, Pithoragarh, India). Tone contrast restricted to the initial syllable could be read as a culminative/accent-like system, but the source does not make that claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 2001 describes the Byangsi of Byans valley, Dharchula tehsil, Pithoragarh district, Uttarakhand, India (speakers from Nabi, Gunji, Napalchu) = Glottolog byan1241 proper. Roka 2009 and Tinkari 2016 describe the Nepal-side varieties (Darchula district; Tinkar/Changru), which Willis 2007 reports the community treats as distinct dialects (Byansi, Tinkari, Kutiyal) of the same language. Krishan 2001 (checked, silent) is Chaudangsi (chau1259), a sister Rung variety that LSI and D.D. Sharma 1989 treat as nearly identical to Byangsi.

The tones typically occur on the first syllable of multisyllabic words only. None of the earlier descriptions mentioned above recorded any tonal contrasts. The examples showing contrasts are given below: /ye/ 'an eagle type of bird' /y\e/ 'mountain' /khu/ 'family' /kh\u/ 'smoke' /pi/ 'four' /p\î-/ 'to sweep' [...] Tone contrasts with long vowels: /ga:/ 'paddy' /g\a:/ 'wound' [...] [7.4.4 (ii)] The suffix /-yø/ is added to most verb roots with some morphophonemic changes in the verb roots. sources.note: Nothing on stress: phonology (sect. 2.0-2.3, pp.271-281) covers vowels, consonants, clusters and 2.3 'Tonal Contrasts' only. p.280: two-way tonal contrast (high falling vs level); 'The tones typically occur on the first syllable of multisyllabic words only.' p.272: vowels with high falling tone are phonetically shorter. Verb section: most verb roots carry high falling tone; loss of root-final vowel length 'compensated for by a high falling tone'. No word 'stress'/'accent' (except 'grave accent mark') anywhere in the 73 pp.

sources.note: Sect. 2.2.4 Phonology (pp.12-15) gives only consonant/vowel inventories and syllable types (taken from Roka et al. 2007 'Byansi Documentation Programme'); no suprasegmentals, no tone, no stress. 'Tone' appears only for sentence-final question intonation.

sources.citation: Willis, Christina M. 2009. Review of Suhnu Ram Sharma, Byangsi Grammar and Vocabulary (Pune: Deccan College, 2007). Himalayan Linguistics Review 8: 1-5. doi 10.5070/H91224534.
sources.note: p.2: Sharma 2007 'describes a three-way tone contrast (high falling, level, and rising) and nasalization of vowels.. Sharma does not mention the stress pattern found in Byangsi.' p.3: 'Perhaps a discussion of the stress pattern of Byangsi would help elucidate the classification of these nominals'. I.e. second-hand confirmation that the 2007 grammar is also silent on stress; reviewer (Darma specialist) implies a stress pattern exists but does not state it.
